competitions.name: AlpacaEval
competitions.tagline: An automatic evaluator for instruction-following language models, fast, cheap, and highly correlated with humans.
competitions.description: AlpacaEval is an LLM-based automatic evaluation pipeline that measures the win rate of instruction-following models against a reference baseline. It is validated against 20K human annotations and offers length-controlled win rates to mitigate length bias. Run by Stanford's Tatsu Lab, it provides a fast and cheap proxy for human evaluation.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repository, add your model config under src/alpaca_eval/models_configs/<model_name>, run evaluation to generate outputs and leaderboard entries, and open a pull request.
participation.submissionFormat: Model configuration YAML, model outputs JSON, and updated leaderboard CSV.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation is API-based (OpenAI/Anthropic credits). Local model generation can be done via APIs or local GPUs.
participation.verification: CI and manual verification by core maintainers for top-5 models.

competitions.quickstart:
pip install alpaca-eval
export OPENAI_API_KEY=<your_api_key>
alpaca_eval --model_outputs 'example/outputs.json'

problems.name: AlpacaEval 2.0 (Length-Controlled Win Rate)
problems.description: Evaluates models against GPT-4 Turbo using length-controlled win rates to mitigate length bias.

problems.name: AlpacaEval 1.0 (Raw Win Rate)
problems.description: Evaluates models against text-davinci-003 using raw win rates.

competitions.name: CogDL
competitions.tagline: An extensive graph deep learning toolkit and benchmark for node, link, and graph classification.
competitions.description: CogDL is a comprehensive graph deep learning library that provides well-optimized operators and easy-to-use APIs to train and compare GNN models. It hosts public leaderboards across multiple graph tasks including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. Researchers can submit their customized models via pull requests to benchmark against state-of-the-art baselines.

organizer.name: Tsinghua, ZJU, DAMO Academy, and ZHIPU.AI

participation.howToSubmit: Implement your model in `cogdl/models` and add a unit test inside `tests/tasks/` (e.g., `tests/tasks/test_node_classification.py`). Then open a pull request to the main repository.
participation.submissionFormat: Python model implementation and unit test.
participation.computeDetails: Supports GPU training; utilizes optimized operators like GE-SpMM to speed up training and save GPU memory.

competitions.quickstart:
from cogdl import experiment

# Run GCN on Cora dataset
experiment(dataset="cora", model="gcn")

competitions.name: SQuAD
competitions.tagline: The Stanford Question Answering Dataset for reading comprehension and question answering evaluation.
competitions.description: SQuAD is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles. The task is to predict the answer text span or determine if the question is unanswerable, evaluated via CodaLab.

participation.howToSubmit: Upload your dataset and model to CodaLab, then use the `cl mimic` command with the official SQuAD development set UUID to generate predictions.

competitions.quickstart:
# Mimic a SQuAD 1.1 model on your custom dataset using CodaLab CLI
cl mimic 0x8f29fe78ffe545128caccab74eb06c57 <model_submission_uuid> <uuid_of_your_dataset>

problems.name: SQuAD 1.1
problems.description: The initial version of the Stanford Question Answering Dataset containing 100,000+ question-answer pairs where the answer is always a segment of text from the reading passage.

problems.name: SQuAD 2.0
problems.description: SQuAD 2.0 combines the 100,000 questions in SQuAD 1.1 with over 50,000 unanswerable questions written adversarially by crowdworkers.

competitions.name: Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark
competitions.tagline: Evaluate outlier and changepoint detection algorithms on multivariate time series from an industrial testbed.
competitions.description: SKAB is a benchmark designed for evaluating anomaly detection algorithms on multivariate time series data. It features 35 datasets collected from sensors on a physical testbed, covering both outlier (single-point) and changepoint (collective) detection. Algorithms are evaluated using F1-score, False Alarm Rate, Missing Alarm Rate, and Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (NAB) metrics.

participation.howToSubmit: Evaluate your algorithm using the provided Jupyter notebooks or TSAD framework, and present/evaluate on Kaggle.
participation.submissionFormat: Jupyter notebook or Python script evaluating on the SKAB datasets.
participation.computeDetails: Most models can be trained and evaluated on standard CPU or consumer GPU.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/waico/SKAB.git
cd SKAB
poetry install
poetry run jupyter notebook notebooks/isolation_forest.ipynb

competitions.name: Mathematics Distillation Challenge — Equational Theories — Stage 2
competitions.tagline: Generate machine-verifiable Lean 4 proofs or countermodels for equational implications over magmas.
competitions.description: A competition based on Terence Tao's Equational Theories Project. Participants submit a Python solver to prove or disprove equational implications over magmas, producing machine-verifiable Lean 4 certificates. Run by the SAIR Foundation, it features Solo and Marathon tracks with strict token and time budgets.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit a single solver.py file (<= 500 KB) implementing the Solo or Marathon I/O protocol to the official competition platform.
participation.submissionFormat: A single solver.py file containing the solver logic and (for Solo) a PROMPT template constant.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation runs the solver in a Docker sandbox with 2048 MB RAM, 2 CPUs, and no network access.
participation.rounds: Solo track (one problem per subprocess) and Marathon track (N problems per subprocess with a shared global budget)
participation.verification: Deterministic Lean 4 judge compiles and verifies the generated proofs or countermodels.

bash scripts/setup.sh
pip install openai
source .env.judge
python3 scripts/run_harness.py
python3 -m pipeline.runner --submission examples/solo/demos/baseline --problems examples/problems/sample_20.json

competitions.name: Sutro Problems
competitions.tagline: Optimize algorithms and neural networks for physical data movement and energy efficiency.
competitions.description: A collection of small, self-contained benchmarks used to evaluate energy-efficient learning and computation. Algorithms are priced by physical data movement on a geometric grid using simplified versions of Bill Dally's model, where arithmetic is free but moving data costs energy.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request against main adding your .ir and generator under submissions/ and updating the accuracy band (table row) it improves.
participation.submissionFormat: A straight-line program (an IR) in the specified instruction set, along with a generator script and a report.
participation.computeDetails: Matmul, symmetry, and sparse-parity are scored symbolically or via CPU simulation. MNIST requires an A100 GPU for energy/time measurements or uses the spatial-computer model.
participation.verification: Symbolic correctness check and static read-cost calculation for matmul/sparse-parity; NVML energy measurement on A100 or word-node hop count in spatial-computer model for MNIST.

competitions.name: Agent Anvil Public Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Compare final-answer-only checks with trace-aware Agent Anvil assertions across tool-use safety scenarios.
competitions.description: Agent Anvil is a public leaderboard for evaluating AI agents on tool-use safety scenarios. It compares traditional final-answer-only checks against trace-aware assertions. Submissions are validated via GitHub Actions and artifact attestations to ensure provenance without executing arbitrary code.

participation.howToSubmit: Run Agent Anvil in your repository, export the leaderboard JSON, and open a pull request adding it to the submissions/ directory.
participation.submissionFormat: JSON file generated via `anvil leaderboard export`
participation.computeDetails: The leaderboard does not execute agents. Users run benchmarks on their own compute and submit attested JSON results.
participation.verification: CI validates submissions, checks GitHub Actions run URLs, and verifies GitHub artifact attestations.

competitions.quickstart:
uv run anvil paper reproduce
uv run anvil leaderboard export docs/paper/results.json \
  --manifest experiments/paper.yaml \
  --out leaderboard_submission.json \
  --agent-name "My Agent" \
  --agent-version "2026-05-22" \
  --repo-url "https://github.com/acme/my-agent" \
  --commit-sha "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
uv run anvil leaderboard validate leaderboard_submission.json

records.description: llm.c baseline; baseline/reference port, no specific speed-up trick.
Tuned learning rate and rotary embeddings.
Pad embeddings, ReLU2, zero-init projections, QK-norm.
Untied token embedding and LM head.
Value/embedding skip connections, momentum warmup, logit softcap.
Sparsified value embeddings, improved rotary embeddings, dropped one attention layer.
Transposed one MLP matrix and added a symmetric matmul kernel.
Optimized distributed training, improved skip-connection gating, enhanced bfloat16 usage.
Smeared token embeddings one position forward.
Asynchronous data fetch/indexing and final-layer validation attention window extension.
Dropped first attention layer, extended long validation windows, updated schedule.
Updated Adam params every other step and reduced batch size.
Backout changes, hyperparameter tuning, lambda padding optimization.
Updated NorMuon learning rate and step logic.
Refined skip architecture, updated exponential decay init.
Sped up Muon, pre-multiplied lambda, reshaped matrices, updated lr and NorMuon axis.
Extended Cautious Weight Decay to Adam parameters.
Computed cross entropy in BF16 during training.
Multiplied attention lambda with weight instead of data, fixed warmup.
NPU-optimized Cautious Weight Decay on Adam: fused RMSNorm/rotary, buffer reuse, bfloat16 weights, a 2070-step schedule, and reduced validation/metrics overhead.

competitions.name: SWE-bench Pro Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Evaluate coding agents on 731 real-world software engineering tasks from SWE-bench Pro.
competitions.description: SWE-bench Pro Leaderboard evaluates the ability of coding agents to resolve real-world software engineering problems. Submissions are evaluated by running the project's test suite in Docker to verify bug fixes without regressions. It is orchestrated by the RDI Foundation using the Green Agent and Amber CLI.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repository, configure scenario.json5 with your Agentbeats ID, add API keys as secrets, and open a PR to main. Alternatively, submit directly via agentbeats.dev.
participation.verification: CI runs the patch in a Docker container and executes the test suite

competitions.quickstart:
amber compile scenario.json5 --docker-compose amber-out
cp amber-out/env.example amber-out/.env
AMBER_CONFIG_CODING_AGENT__MODEL_NAME=gpt-4o \
AMBER_CONFIG_CODING_AGENT__OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-xxx \
docker compose -f amber-out/compose.yaml --env-file amber-out/.env up

problems.description: 731 real-world software engineering tasks.
